title: Three-Factor Learning and Synaptic Consolidation in Cortex

html:
Three-factor learning is the natural next step after voltage- and calcium-dependent coincidence rules. The previous subsection described how cortical synapses compute a local eligibility trace from presynaptic timing, postsynaptic voltage trajectories, dendritic nonlinearities, and compartment-specific Ca2+^{2+} dynamics. The three-factor formalism adds a second stage: a synapse first writes an eligibility trace eie_i, and only later is that trace converted into lasting change if an additional modulatory or circuit-level factor M(t)M(t) arrives, so that Δwi∝eiM(t)\Delta w_i \propto e_i M(t). In molecular terms, this second stage can be implemented through mechanisms such as CaMKII-dependent tagging, cAMP/PKA signaling, and synaptic tagging-and-capture (STC), while neuromodulator receptor pharmacology determines how a given modulatory input reshapes STDP windows, plasticity thresholds, and consolidation probability. This formalism relates closely to the precision-weighting story from predictive coding: the third factor does not merely “permit” learning, but helps determine which locally computed errors are important enough to be converted into persistent synaptic change.

An important feature of cortical three-factor learning is that the eligibility trace is not a signless memory of “something happened.” Cortical synapses can preserve which direction of future change is currently eligible–for example, whether the stored trace is poised for LTP-like strengthening or LTD-like weakening 1. Moreover, the same pre-existing eligibility trace can be converted with opposite signs depending on which neuromodulator arrives: in visual cortex, norepinephrine transforms such traces toward potentiation, whereas serotonin transforms them toward depression 2. The “third factor” also need not be a diffuse monoamine in the narrow sense. Interneuron-mediated disinhibition can play an equivalent gating role by determining whether dendritic coincidence signals are allowed to produce a plasticity-permissive voltage/Ca2+^{2+} state. This provides a bridge back to dendritic credit-assignment models such as Sacramento et al.: the local voltage and apical–basal mismatch machinery writes the synaptic eligibility trace, but whether that trace is ultimately expressed depends on additional modulatory or circuit-level state.

This is why cortex needs three-factor learning rather than Hebbian coincidence alone. Purely Hebbian rules are too myopic: they can register local covariation, but they cannot by themselves solve delayed credit assignment, distinguish salient from irrelevant coincidences, or regulate when transient errors should be committed to long-term storage. Three-factor learning is a general biological motif, but its cortical implementation is unusually shaped by laminar architecture, pyramidal-cell dendritic geometry, feedback pathways, and local disinhibitory motifs. In cortex, the eligibility trace written at a synapse is already compartment-specific: apical tuft synapses may encode local coactivity and branch-level context, whereas basal synapses may encode output-referenced coincidence. The task of this subsection is therefore to show how cortical architecture–its lamination, dendritic compartmentalization, interneuron motifs, and regionally varying neuromodulator distributions–determines which three-factor rules operate where, when, and under what precision regime. A preprint examines norepinephrine and synaptic efficacy (Figure) 90. The preprint tests a role for astrocyte calcium signals (Figure).

Cortical eligibility traces are themselves tuned to cortical computation. In cortex, experimentally inferred eligibility windows are on the order of ∼5\sim 5–1010 s, substantially longer than the ∼1\sim 1–22 s windows typically demonstrated in striatum 3, 1, 4, 5. That longer window is well matched to cortical working memory, multi-step sensory inference, and planning, and it also compensates for the fact that cortical dopamine and other modulators often arrive through slower and more diffuse volume transmission than the tightly timed dopaminergic signals seen in striatal microcircuits. In prefrontal cortex, recurrent activity may extend the functional credit-assignment window even beyond the molecular lifetime of the trace itself, creating a hybrid mechanism in which a labile molecular eligibility trace is sustained or re-instantiated by persistent network activity 6.

The regional distribution of third-factor control across cortex is best understood not as a set of simple spatial gradients, but as a multidimensional receptor-and-innervation landscape. The cleanest way to summarize that landscape is as follows:

Dopamine

Main article: Dopamine

Cortical dopamine is not organized by a single “more anterior = more dopaminergic” rule. Rather, it varies along partly dissociable maps of axonal innervation density, receptor density per neuron, and degree of behavioral dependence on dopaminergic third-factor gating 7. In primates, dopaminergic fiber density is especially high in agranular cortex—including motor cortex, anterior cingulate, and insula—whereas more granular regions such as dorsolateral PFC and occipital cortex often show lower density and more bilaminar patterns of innervation 8, 9. D1 receptors are the dominant cortical dopamine receptor class in macaque neocortex, with D1 density far exceeding D2 density overall, although D2 receptors remain widespread and are not restricted to frontal cortex 10, 11, 12.

Functionally, dopamine is sparse or episodic rather than absent in early sensory cortex, where it can gate salience- and value-weighted remapping and consolidation 13, 14, 15. In motor cortex, dopamine is one of the clearest cortical examples of an RL-style third factor, required for motor-skill acquisition and learning-related reorganization of local circuits 16, 17. In lateral PFC and ACC, dopamine shifts from an occasional consolidation gate to an online regulator of learning state, flexibility, effort allocation, and self-initiated action control 18, 19, 20, 21, 22. A 2026 mouse study examines dopamine-sensitive motor-cortical circuits (Figure) 87. The study measures dopamine dynamics during movement and reward (Figure). The mouse study examines movement vigor (Figure). The experiment also varies reward availability (Figure).

Acetylcholine

Main article: Acetylcholine

Cortical acetylcholine is broadly available across neocortex, but its distribution is also not captured by a simple gradient. Cholinergic innervation is biased toward limbic/paralimbic and downstream association territory, whereas primary visual cortex is relatively cholino-poor 23, 24. The receptor map is, however, partly dissociable from the raw supply map: some muscarinic receptor classes peak in sensory cortex in absolute density, but when normalized per neuron, cholinergic receptor expression generally increases from sensory to higher-order cortex 25.

In early sensory cortex, acetylcholine often acts as a major online teaching signal that converts attentional selection into map reorganization and perceptual learning 26, 27, 28, 29. In prefrontal and cingulate cortex, by contrast, acetylcholine functions less like a scalar reward signal and more like a state-setting gate 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35.

Serotonin

Main article: Serotonin

Serotonergic axons are broadly distributed across primate cortex, so cortical specialization appears to arise more from receptor topology and receptor-specific sign than from whether serotonin reaches a region at all 36, 25. A particularly important receptor gradient is 5-HT1A5\text{-HT}_{1A}, which is enriched in anterior cingulate, default-mode, and salience-network territory and relatively weak in motor and visual cortex 25. Meanwhile, 5-HT2A5\text{-HT}_{2A} is concentrated on pyramidal-cell apical dendrites, especially in layers II/III and V/VI, giving serotonin direct access to the same dendritic compartments that carry top-down and error-like signals 37. A parallel route runs through interneurons, as 5-HT35\text{-HT}_{3} receptors are largely confined to cortical GABAergic interneurons 38, 39.

Functionally, serotonin is one of the clearest examples of a neuromodulator that can set the sign of plasticity: in visual cortex, delayed serotonergic input converts eligibility traces into LTD-like weakening, opposite to norepinephrine’s potentiating effect 2, 1. Primate V1 is a notable sensory exception with unusually prominent serotonergic receptor machinery, whereas frontal and orbitofrontal cortex use serotonin more strongly as a flexibility- and contingency-switching gate 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45.

Norepinephrine

Main article: Norepinephrine

Noradrenergic fibers are broadly distributed across cortical layers, with especially high innervation in primary sensorimotor cortex and more uniform innervation across limbic/paralimbic cortex 46, 8. The sharper specialization comes from which locus coeruleus (LC) subpopulation is recruited, in what firing mode, and onto which receptor-defined microcircuit 47, 48. In prefrontal cortex, α1\alpha_1, α2\alpha_2, and β\beta receptors occupy different laminar compartments, giving noradrenergic modulation different access to apical, associational, and feedforward-recipient strata 49. Norepinephrine can also act in a compartment-specific way within a single area, as in auditory cortex where it differentially regulates apical versus basal inhibition onto pyramidal dendrites 50.

Functionally, NE is a strong third factor for salience- and novelty-gated potentiation in sensory cortex, a task-timed plasticity gate in motor cortex, and a precision- and state-setting signal in PFC 2, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58.

Mu-opioid receptors

Mu-opioid receptors are relatively enriched in cingulate, insular, and prefrontal cortex, where they modulate reinforcement, valuation, and affective processing. They likely provide an additional third-factor signal for pain- and reward-related plasticity, especially in circuits where motivational salience is tightly coupled to affective state 59.

These neuromodulator-specific maps are not arbitrary. Large-scale receptor mapping shows that cortical receptor landscapes form principal gradients aligned with the unimodal-to-transmodal hierarchy, while additional gradients capture modality-specific and circuit-specific specializations 60, 61. The implication is that the third factor at a cortical synapse is not a single scalar neuromodulatory variable but a composite vector: which modulators arrive, at what concentration, onto which receptor subtypes, in which laminar and dendritic compartments, under which local inhibitory state. That composite vector determines whether an existing eligibility trace is converted into potentiation, depression, consolidation, or no lasting change at all. A 2025 study examines adolescent mouse frontal-cortex plasticity (Figure) 88. The study manipulates dopamine-receptor signaling (Figure).

Cortical three-factor learning is also implemented through disinhibitory circuit motifs. The canonical example is the VIP →\rightarrow SST →\rightarrow pyramidal-dendrite motif. Across neocortex, VIP interneurons preferentially inhibit SST interneurons; SST cells provide major dendritic and apical inhibition onto pyramidal neurons; and long-range feedback, behavioral-state, and reinforcement-related signals can recruit VIP cells 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67. The net effect is a transient removal of the SST-imposed dendritic veto, increasing the probability that coincident feedback and feedforward input will generate the dendritic voltage and Ca2+^{2+} signals required for associative plasticity. This is not merely a theoretical possibility: activating VIP cells or silencing SST cells is sufficient to open associative LTP in mouse olfactory cortex, and engaging the same motif enhances adult plasticity in V1 62, 63, 68. It is therefore useful to regard dendritic disinhibition as a circuit-level third factor: not the eligibility trace itself, but a context-specific gate on whether locally written eligibility is allowed to become lasting plasticity (but also whether eligibility will be computed in the first place).

Related cortex-wide gradients in interneuron composition further bias which kinds of three-factor rules dominate in different territories. Across human and macaque cortex, the most consistent tradeoff is not total inhibition but a relative SST↔\leftrightarrowPVALB balance: SST is relatively enriched in orbitofrontal, medial prefrontal, anterior insular, and temporal association cortex, whereas PVALB is relatively enriched in unimodal somatomotor, parietal, and visual cortex 69, 70, 71. Since PV interneurons primarily target the soma and perisomatic compartment, they are well suited for fast gain and temporal-precision control, whereas SST interneurons preferentially target distal and apical dendrites, where they regulate top-down input, dendritic nonlinearities, and plasticity 72, 73, 74, 75. This suggests a cortex-wide plasticity bias: PV-richer unimodal cortex is biased toward fast somatic precision control, whereas SST-richer association cortex is biased toward dendritic and apical gating of integrative plasticity.

Synaptic consolidation is the slower selection stage of this cortical plasticity process. Here, the story is not just “strong events consolidate, weak events do not.” Rather, early voltage/Ca2+^{2+}- and three-factor plasticity write a labile tagged state at recently active cortical synapses, and persistence depends on whether those tagged synapses can capture sufficient plasticity-related products (PRPs) within the relevant temporal and spatial window 76, 77. Strong events usually persist because they both set tags and drive PRP synthesis; weak events may still set tags, but are stabilized only if PRPs are supplied by nearby strong events, neuromodulator-dependent protein-synthesis signals, or later reactivation (e.g through spaced repetition) that refreshes tags and recruits additional PRPs. Consolidation is therefore a selection, capture, and reinforcement process, not a simple threshold: tagged synapses can cooperate or compete for limited stabilizing resources, and repeated/spaced reactivation can increase the probability of persistence by re-opening effective capture windows 77, 78, 79. This capture can also be branch-local rather than neuron-global, consistent with local dendritic protein synthesis and branch-specific persistent plasticity 80, 81, 82. A 2025 hippocampal-slice study tests synaptic tagging and capture (Figure) 89. The hippocampal study examines neighboring synapses (Figure).

The computational consequences are substantial. First, cortical storage is precision-weighted: the third factor does not merely allow plasticity, but helps decide which cortical prediction errors are worth committing to long-term change. In humans, cortical unsigned prediction errors are precision-weighted in a dopamine-dependent manner, and in auditory cortex acetylcholine sharpens prediction-error responses 83, 84. Second, three-factor rules solve temporal credit assignment on cortical timescales: second-long eligibility traces, supplemented in PFC by persistent activity, allow delayed outcomes to update the synapses that were actually causal 1, 3, 6. Third, branch-local consolidation supports low-interference memory allocation, because different latent causes or task variables can be stabilized on different dendritic branches rather than indiscriminately across the whole neuron 80, 82. Finally, in frontal and especially motor cortex, reward- and outcome-gated three-factor rules can be interpreted as approximations of policy gradient updates 85, 86, 17.

The overall picture is consistent with the rest of the cortical optimization architecture developed so far. The previous subsection explained how cortex writes compartment-specific eligibility traces through local voltage and Ca2+^{2+} dynamics. This subsection shows how cortex decides which of those candidate updates should count: through neuromodulator-specific receptor landscapes, laminar and dendritic specialization, disinhibitory circuit motifs, and branch-local consolidation machinery. Cortex does not invent a qualitatively new biochemistry for each region. Instead, it overlays a shared molecular eligibility system with a multidimensional receptor-and-interneuron landscape whose principal axes track the cortical hierarchy and whose local deviations implement modality- and circuit-specific specializations. The result is a cortex-wide family of three-factor learning rules in which the “third factor” is best understood not as a single scalar broadcast, but as a structured, regionally tuned control vector that converts local cortical errors into selective long-term change. See "Neuromodulators" for a broader treatment of what variables each neuromodulatory subsystem may encode (and how evolution purpose-built each subsystem).
